=== BEGIN PAPER (MD) ===
# SINGULARITY OF THE HESSIAN IN DEEP LEARNING

# Levent Sagun

Mathematics Department

New York University

sagun@cims.nyu.edu

# Léon Bottou

Facebook AI Research

New York

leon@bottou.org

# Yann LeCun

Computer Science Department

New York University

yann@cs.nyu.edu

# ABSTRACT

We look at the eigenvalues of the Hessian of a loss function before and after training. The eigenvalue distribution is seen to be composed of two parts, the bulk which is concentrated around zero, and the edges which are scattered away from zero. We present empirical evidence for the bulk indicating how overparametrized the system is, and for the edges indicating the complexity of the input data.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

Given a (piece-wise) differentiable loss function, and a gradient based algorithm to minimize it, the knowledge of the second order information about it can tell us quite a bit about how the landscape looks like, and how we could modify our algorithm to make it go faster and find better solutions. But, one of the biggest challenges in second order optimization methods is in accessing that second order information itself. In particular, in deep learning there have been many proposals to accelerate training using second order information. Ngiam et al. (2011) has an in depth review of some of the proposals for approximating the Hessian of the loss function. Nevertheless, given the computational complexity of the problems at hand, we don't have much information on what the actual Hessian looks like. This work is part of a series of papers that explore the data-model-algorithm connection along with Sagun et al. (2014; 2015) and it builds on top of the intuition developed in Lecun et al. (1998).

In this short note, we show how the data and the architecture depends on the eigenvalues of the Hessian of the loss function. In particular, we observe that the top discrete eigenvalues depend on the data, and the bulk of the eigenvalues depend on the architecture. Furthermore, as we keep growing the size of the network, we observe that the discrete part that depends on data remains the same, but the concentration around zero sharpens.

There are various conclusions and implications of this singularity. Recent research suggest new insights into convergence properties of gradient based algorithms in non-convex systems (Lee et al., 2016; Hardt et al., 2015). The results come together with their implications on neural networks. However, the proofs require the system at hand to be non-degenerate. An immediate conclusion of our observation is that the Hessian of the loss function is very singular. Therefore, a lot of the theory and methodology that assumes non-singular Hessian cannot be applied without an appropriate modification.

# 2 MNIST EIGENVALUES ON A FULLY-CONNECTED MODEL

We calculate the exact Hessian of the loss function of a network with two hidden layers. The inputs are  $28 \times 28$  MNIST data, the network has two hidden layers with ReLU nonlinearity, the top layer has a softmax and a negative log likelihood loss function at the end. We plot the histogram of the eigenvalues of the Hessian for a varying number of hidden units. The Hessian turns out to be extremely singular, and increasing the number of units in hidden layers only add to the singularity of the Hessian.

![](images/72b110c15e35d079fd4be919c35b8e8004aac76c4b6665cc45301fb322bb9776.jpg)  
Figure 1: (left) Full Hessian matrix for one of the systems. (right) Eigenvalue profile for increasingly bigger networks.

# 2.1 VARYING THE DATA

To demonstrate how the eigenvalue distribution may depend on data itself, we keep the same architecture and change the inputs to random patterns. Initially, a random point in the weight space is selected, and we calculated the Hessian without any training. After training the system until the norm of the gradient is close to zero. We again calculate the exact Hessian and plot the histogram of their eigenvalues.

![](images/0d4aec1f047b1ac3cec12ac19650953ea794c56dc8dd8de9ee8baa2c15bf71a7.jpg)  
Figure 2: Comparing random input (last two) with the MNIST data (first). Initial eigenvalue profiles are very different, as well as the final profile when compared to figure 1.

# 3 A SIMPLER CASE

In this section, we will repeat the same experiment in two-dimensional data, in an attempt to understand better the connection between the data and the spectrum of the Hessian. We create two Gaussian blobs, centered at  $(1,1)$  and  $(-1, - 1)$ , and first we keep the standard deviation the same, and increase the network size.

![](images/5012d4c692a670c82eea0d4d115c37c9177bc18d304eb2d65d586ea0846a1cef.jpg)  
Figure 3: The input data for the simple case.

The network architecture is the same, two hidden layer fully connected network, with ReLU nonlinearities and a softmax at the top layer combined with a negative log-likelihood loss function. We train the system with gradient descent with constant step size. At the end of the training the norm of the gradient is at the order of  $10^{-4}$ .

![](images/bd0022a2dcba211d53f981a7a3627e1fc06abd084f572f816b0bfe33eef277e7.jpg)  
Figure 4: Increasing the network size: Systems with 18, 74, 162, 282, and 434 parameters, resp.

There are two eigenvalues that are isolated, and away from the bulk of the spectrum. Increasing the network only adds to the concentration of eigenvalues at and around zero. To give an insight into how the Hessian's themselves look like, here we plot the full Hessian matrices for three of the systems above:

![](images/770b473e5289e062bdae64ce87491e1dafae10a1b8c23c74dd9b182e9ecfc021.jpg)  
Rotated Hessian Matrix  
Figure 5: Hessian heatmaps for 18, 74 and 162 paramters systems. The plots are 90 degrees rotates counter-clock wise.

All of the training has been done with random initializations on the weight space with the same standard deviation. In other words, initial points are randomly chosen on the surface of a sphere with a fixed radius given the total number of parameters. This begs the question of the effect of the choice of the initial point. Therefore, now we fix the network size, and repeat the experiment with different random initializations over 5K times, and plot the fluctuations of the top eigenvalue.

![](images/b0fdef03c957744ffd5ce6f98917de789e27a184dc02999e0f88dfcd1e8e9493.jpg)  
Figure 6: Top eigenvalue fluctuations over 5000 runs of the same system with same data and algorithm but different initial points.

The next question is how the spectrum responds to the increased complexity of data. To this end, we keep the architecture the same, and increase the standard deviation of the two Gaussian blobs. They are still centered at the same two points, but it becomes harder to separate them as they merge together. Gradient descent still converges to a low-cost value, but the error is higher, and it can't learn how to separate them perfectly as the blobs merge together. We observe that the top two eigenvalues grow significantly, and beyond its natural fluctuations due to the initialization.

![](images/5253dbc7877655eeec058777cfb5863446af786902753386eec5c41f330781aa.jpg)  
Figure 7: Response of the top eigenvalues to the increased complexity of data. The numbers on top of the figures indicate the standard deviation of the Gaussian blobs. Their means are kept the same at  $(1,1)$  and  $(-1, -1)$ , respectively.

# 4 CONCLUSION

We show that the Hessian of the loss functions in deep learning is degenerate. This has implications on the theoretical work which requires improvements in its premises. One such step has been taken in Panageas & Piliouras (2016) in relaxing the isolated singularity condition that was assumed in Lee et al. (2016). From a practical point of view this has multiple implications:

- The landscape may be flat beyond the notion of wide basins.  
- Training goes to a place with small gradient, but it is not zero.  
- There are still negative eigenvalues even when they are small in magnitude.

This suggests that we may be able to look beyond the classical notions of basins when exploring the energy landscapes of loss functions. Next obvious question is to find low energy paths between solutions to show the kind of flatness in such landscapes. This will be explored in a subsequent work in the same series.

We also demonstrate the two phases of the spectrum, one that is concentrated around zero that depends on the size of the model, and the second part that is away from the bulk of the spectrum, that is isolated and depends on the data.

This kind of two-phased non-degeneracy can, in fact, be a desirable property. A degenerate Hessian implies locally flat regions. A degenerate Hessian at the scale that we observe in deep learning may imply flat regions across space, at the global scale.

- We can devise separate methods for the directions that correspond to the top eigenvalues.  
- We can take advantage of the directions that correspond to the zero or small eigenvalues by attempting to find paths of low energies in the weight space.

As a first step to the last item, initial experiments are promising: Let's take a random point on the weight space and train two systems from that point: (1) with gradient descent, and (2) with stochastic gradient descent. At each step, take a straight line between the two points and interpolate the cost value. The resulting profile is completely flat even when the points keep diverging from one another. Next, take two random initial points on the weight space, so now they are orthogonal to each other. And train two systems with different shuffling of data for SGD. This time one would expect the line interpolation to give arbitrary values since the initial points are completely orthogonal, surprisingly, the line interpolation also decreases albeit not as flat as the previous one.

![](images/3612f0e2493d1acfe6dac0c3cc8556f0fc8dcd1d8a54da2cbf88186e6ec84592.jpg)  
Figure 8:  $z$ -axis is the distance between points. The left most and right most curves in each plot are actual training profiles, and the lines in between are interpolations only. (left figure) same initial point (right figure) random (hence orthogonal) initial points.

![](images/b1422139794056c8cd5c8eb0a7c8df98d3b8ab767e9b3e19e0eea44d71bd7fb1.jpg)

# ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

We would like to thank Afonso Bandeira, Yann Dauphin, Ruoyu Sun, Arthur Szlam and Soumith Chintala for valuable discussions. Part of the research has been conducted when the first author was an intern at FAIR.

# REFERENCES

Yann Lecun, Leon Bottou, Genevieve B Orr, and Klaus-Robert Müller. Efficient backprop. 1998.

Jiquan Ngiam, Adam Coates, Ahbik Lahiri, Bobby Prochnow, Quoc V Le, and Andrew Y Ng. On optimization methods for deep learning. In Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML-11), pp. 265-272, 2011.

Reviewer dimension: QUAL  
Paper summary: This short note studies the Hessian spectrum of a deep network loss, comparing eigenvalues before vs. after training. The main empirical claim is a “two-phase” spectrum: (i) a bulk concentrated near zero whose shape changes with architecture/overparameterization, and (ii) a set of isolated “edge” eigenvalues further from zero that depends on the data. Experiments include MNIST with an FC-ReLU-softmax model, input randomization vs. trained MNIST, and a synthetic 2D Gaussian-blobs classification setup where network size and data separability are varied.

Strengths:
- Focused technical investigation of Hessian eigenvalue distributions with an attempt to isolate factors (architecture vs. data vs. initialization).
- Uses exact Hessians in the tractable fully-connected ReLU MNIST setting and in a smaller 2D toy problem, enabling direct spectrum visualization rather than approximation.
- Includes some robustness exploration via multiple random initializations (5K runs) in the toy problem and a qualitative interpolation experiment between different trained solutions.

Weaknesses:
- Methodological clarity is limited: key implementation details (training hyperparameters, step sizes, optimizer settings, stopping criteria, how gradients are measured, and how Hessian eigenvalues are computed numerically) are mostly missing or too implicit for technical soundness verification.
- The paper provides limited quantitative evidence beyond histograms/plots; claims such as “top discrete eigenvalues depend on data” are not backed by systematic quantitative comparisons (e.g., measured eigenvalue statistics with error bars/variance comparisons).
- Comparisons/positioning: the note does not rigorously compare to the most relevant recent “Hessian singularity” / spectral analyses beyond a cursory literature list; it reads more like empirical observations than a methodologically competitive study.
- Reproducibility is weak: no code, no precise network specs (layer widths for MNIST beyond “varying number of hidden units”), no explicit dataset splits, and no information sufficient to reproduce the exact Hessian-eigen computations.
- Statistical rigor is limited: except for one qualitative/visual eigenvalue fluctuation figure over many runs, most other results appear single-run or without confidence intervals / significance tests.

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- QUAL-MET: strength: The conceptual experiment design (compare Hessian before/after training; vary architecture; vary data; vary initialization; inspect 2D case for interpretability) is aligned with the stated hypotheses about data/architecture dependence of eigenvalues. The observation that increasing width sharpens concentration near zero is plausible given overparameterization/degeneracy narratives.  
  weakness: Several technical points are underspecified in the extract, making it hard to verify methodological correctness:
  - “We calculate the exact Hessian” is claimed, but the paper extract does not state the exact definition of the Hessian (full-data loss vs. mini-batch loss; regularization; loss scaling), nor how it is computed for ReLU networks (handling non-differentiability at kink points—ReLU is piecewise linear and Hessians are often zero except at points where activations switch). That matters for whether the Hessian is “singular” due to model structure vs. due to numerical implementation.
  - The MNIST model includes ReLU; exact Hessian of the network output composed with cross-entropy can be nontrivial, but the extract does not specify whether they use the Hessian of the empirical loss over the full dataset or a subset.
  - Numerical details for eigenvalue computation are absent (e.g., full eigendecomposition vs. partial spectrum; how many eigenvalues are computed; conditioning issues), and thus whether “bulk vs edge” is an artifact of computation or plotting choices cannot be assessed.
- QUAL-EXP: strength: Experiments directly vary (a) network size, (b) data distribution (MNIST vs random patterns; Gaussian blob separability), and (c) initialization. There is an attempt to relate Hessian eigenvalues to learning difficulty (harder separation increases top eigenvalues). The 2D toy problem allows clearer interpretation (isolated eigenvalues with increasing data complexity).  
  weakness: The evaluation is largely qualitative:
  - Most plots are histograms without reporting summary statistics (e.g., bulk width/variance, proportion of eigenvalues near zero, location of spectral edges) or uncertainty estimates.
  - Missing standard datasets/benchmarks expectations are not central because this is a Hessian-spectral note, but it still needs stronger quantitative validation for its core claims.
  - No ablations addressing critical confounders: loss definition, regularization, weight initialization scale, stopping tolerance effects, or ReLU implementation choices (e.g., whether training reaches regions with fixed activation patterns).
  - The figure about interpolation flatness (Figure 8) is intriguing but not technically validated: no quantitative correlation to Hessian null-space/near-null-space dimensions, and no systematic comparison of GD vs SGD settings beyond the anecdotal outcomes described.
- QUAL-REP: strength: The paper is at least conceptually reproducible in outline (datasets: MNIST + 2D Gaussians; architecture class: two hidden layer FC; training via gradient descent/SGD; measure Hessian eigenvalues pre/post training). The toy problem includes a strong statement about 5K random initializations.  
  weakness: Reproducibility is poor based on the extract:
  - No code availability statement.
  - No hyperparameters: learning rates/step size (except “constant step size” and gradient norm threshold “order of 1e-4” in the toy setup), number of epochs/iterations, batch size, and optimizer details are missing for MNIST and underspecified in toy.
  - No precise architecture sizes for MNIST (exact number of hidden units per histogram) or training settings.
  - No dataset split description (train vs test is not discussed); for Hessian of loss it matters whether the Hessian is computed on the full dataset, training set, or a batch.
  - “Exact Hessian” and eigenvalue computations need numeric details (implementation approach, computational feasibility constraints, and whether eigenvalues are computed fully or approximately).
- QUAL-CMP: strength: The introduction cites relevant work on second-order optimization approximations and convergence analyses in nonconvex systems, and the conclusion references relaxing isolated critical point assumptions. The positioning is reasonable as a “short note” of empirical evidence.  
  weakness: It does not provide a robust comparison to closest prior empirical/theoretical Hessian spectrum studies (not in the extract besides a broad mention). Given the paper’s specific empirical spectrum decomposition claim, one would expect more direct comparison to known Hessian spectral analyses or theoretical results on Hessian degeneracy/flat directions in overparameterized networks, including whether those works observe similar “edge/bulk” separation. The extract also cites “Eigenvalues of the Hessian in Deep Learning: Singularity and Beyond” (from the provided references list), but the paper extract does not show a concrete comparison against that work’s setup/metrics.
- QUAL-STA: strength: The toy experiment includes a 5000-run initialization study for the top eigenvalue fluctuations, which is a form of statistical validation (variance across random seeds).

Paper summary: The paper studies the Hessian eigenvalue spectrum of deep networks (exact Hessian computation for a small fully-connected ReLU model on MNIST). It reports a “two-phase” spectrum: a bulk concentrated near (and sharpening toward) zero and a smaller set of isolated eigenvalues away from zero. It further explores how (i) changing data versus (ii) changing network size affects which parts of the spectrum: isolated/top eigenvalues appear data-dependent, while the near-zero bulk is more architecture-dependent; increasing model size concentrates more eigenvalues around zero. In a 2D toy setting with two Gaussian blobs, the authors vary network size and input separability/complexity, observing persistent isolated eigenvalues and growth in the top eigenvalues as data complexity increases. The paper concludes that the Hessian is highly degenerate/singular in deep learning, with implications for theory that assumes non-degenerate Hessians, and offers practical speculation about flat energy landscapes and low-energy paths.

Strengths:
- Tackles an important conceptual question: how curvature (via Hessian eigenvalues) behaves in overparameterized deep networks, and what aspects depend on data vs. model.
- Provides empirical evidence (plots and experiments) for a “bulk + outliers” spectral structure and for increasing degeneracy with model size, motivating a rethinking of non-singularity assumptions in optimization theory.
- The work is grounded in controlled comparisons (MNIST vs random patterns; network size; toy data complexity; repeated random initializations), which strengthens the credibility that the observed spectral phases are not merely anecdotal.

Weaknesses:
- The practical significance is limited by scope: results are shown for small fully-connected ReLU networks with exact Hessians; there is no demonstration that the spectral findings translate into improved algorithms, acceleration, or better generalization on standard benchmarks.
- “State-of-the-art improvement” is not really addressed: the submission is primarily analytical/empirical, without comparison to existing methods that use curvature information, nor quantitative evidence that the insights lead to better optimization performance.
- Societal/real-world impact is essentially absent: no discussion of who benefits/harmed, fairness, robustness, or deployment considerations; the contribution is mostly theoretical about loss landscapes.

Detailed assessment by sub-dimension:
- SIGN-BRD: strength: The paper advances understanding of deep learning optimization by proposing/confirming a potentially general structural property of the loss Hessian (degenerate bulk with data-dependent outliers). This could influence multiple lines of work in optimization theory, convergence analysis, and landscape interpretation. weakness: The evidence is limited to particular architectures/losses and small-scale settings (exact Hessians). Without broader validation across architectures (e.g., CNNs/Transformers) or training regimes, the breadth of influence on the broader community remains plausible but not firmly established.
